summary: Defines how to use MPLS to route header-compressed packets over a label switched path. Header compression cuts packet overhead and, with MPLS, improves bandwidth efficiency and scalability. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Packets carry long address labels. This note shows how to shrink those labels on a link while a fast delivery system still moves them along.

subtitle: How to carry header-compressed packets across an MPLS network without decompressing at every router.

tldr.problem: Voice over IP packets carry headers of at least 48 bytes for payloads that are often no more than 30 bytes, and compressing and decompressing at every hop does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: A compressor and decompressor are joined by an MPLS pseudowire that carries only compressed packets, set up with LDP and configured by reusing PPP header compression options, with a small HC control parameter before each packet.
tldr.outcome: Compressed packets cross the label switched path untouched, saving bandwidth and letting more compressed flows be handled.

today: RFC 4901 is a Proposed Standard, published in June 2007. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Voice over IP typically uses voice/RTP/UDP/IP encapsulation, and MPLS labels are added on top. With MPLS VPNs and label stacking, the total packet header in the simplest IPv4 case is at least 48 bytes while the voice payload is often no more than 30 bytes. With IPv6 the header is even larger relative to the payload.

Header compression (HC) cuts that overhead using schemes such as ECRTP and ROHC. This RFC makes it possible to route HC packets over an MPLS label switched path (LSP) without compression and decompression cycles at each router, which improves bandwidth efficiency and the number of simultaneous compressed flows each router can handle. The solution uses MPLS pseudowire technology.
sections.eli5: A short note stuck inside a huge envelope wastes paper. Header compression shrinks the envelope, and this RFC lets the shrunken envelope ride the whole trip without being reopened at each stop.

sections.title: How It Fits Together
sections.content:
The ingress router (the compressor) applies HC to the IP packet, the compressed packet is forwarded along an LSP using MPLS labels, and the egress router (the decompressor) restores the header. In the RFC's example, R1/HC compresses, R2 and R3 only switch labels, and R4/HD decompresses. Instead of data/RTP/UDP/IP/MPLS-labels, the LSP carries data/compressed-header/MPLS-labels, often saving more than 90% of the RTP/UDP/IP overhead. HC reduces IP/UDP/RTP headers to 2-4 bytes for most packets.

Compressor and decompressor each keep a context for every flow, and packets mostly carry just a context identifier (CID) plus the hard-to-predict changes. Each pseudowire (PW) acts like a point-to-point link and carries one HC channel using one HC scheme, and only compressed packets, never uncompressed ones. The decompressor finds the right context from the pair of PW label and CID, so two compressors can reuse the same CID without confusion. Because most HC schemes use feedback, a PW is set up in each direction.
sections.eli5: Only the first and last post offices open the shrunk packages. All the post offices in between just read the outside sticker and pass them on.

sections.title: Pseudowire Design Rules
sections.content:
Each compressor-decompressor channel maps to a single PW with two PW labels, one per direction. A single PW label MUST be used for many HC flows (hundreds or thousands) rather than one label per flow, because CID assignment already exists and need not be duplicated. Multiple PWs SHOULD be set up when different quality of service is needed for different compressed streams, since QoS follows the EXP bit marking in the PW label.

The packet stack is the media stream, then the compressed headers, then the HC control parameter (2 octets), then the MPLS label stack of at least 2 labels (8 octets), then the link layer (PPP, PoS or Ethernet). The PW label MUST serve as the demultiplexer at the decompressor, which MUST ensure that the label it distributes for a channel is unique.
sections.eli5: One shared mailbox is used for hundreds of conversations, with each conversation marked by a small number inside. That is simpler than giving every conversation its own mailbox.

sections.title: Signaling and Negotiation
sections.content:
PWs MUST be set up in advance using RFC 4447 control messages exchanged between the compressor and decompressor, over an LDP session using extended discovery, with PW labels distributed in downstream unsolicited mode. The PW type in the FEC object identifies the HC scheme: 0x001A for ROHC, 0x001B for ECRTP, 0x001C for IPHC and 0x001D for CRTP. The same PW type MUST be used in both directions, and an HC PW MUST NOT carry uncompressed flows.

Parameters are carried in the PW Interface Parameters Sub-TLV, reusing configuration options from RFC 3544 (type 0x0F, for CRTP, ECRTP and IPHC) and RFC 3241 (type 0x0D, for ROHC). The PPP negotiation process itself is not reused, only the option formats as descriptors. Which option goes with which PW type is strict. The RFC 3544 option MUST be included for ECRTP, CRTP and IPHC and MUST NOT be included for ROHC, while the RFC 3241 option is the reverse. A decompressor MUST reject a misconfigured option and send an explicit error. Suggested values include a TCP_SPACE and NON_TCP_SPACE of 15, a MAX_HEADER of 168 octets and, for ROHC, a MAX_CID of at most 16383.

Suboption 1 enables RTP compression and MUST be included for CRTP PWs. Suboption 2 enables enhanced RTP compression for ECRTP PWs and MUST NOT appear together with suboption 1. A new suboption 3 allows turning off TCP-only or non-TCP-only compression, which was not possible before because a value of 0 in the space fields means one context.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the two ends agree on the rules, like deciding which secret code they will use. The agreement is written on a standard form that already existed for another kind of link.

sections.title: The HC Control Parameter
sections.content:
Each HC packet starts with a 16-bit HC control parameter: four zero bits, a 4-bit packet type, a 6-bit length and 2 reserved bits. The leading zeros keep the payload from being mistaken for IP, in line with the PW control word encoding, though this is not meant to be a PW control word. Packet types 0 to 10 are defined: ROHC small and large CIDs, FULL_HEADER, the compressed TCP, non-TCP, RTP and UDP forms, and CONTEXT_STATE. Types 11 to 15 are not yet assigned.

The length field exists only for short packets, because Ethernet may pad them. If the MPLS payload is 64 octets or more the length MUST be zero. Otherwise it MUST be the PW payload length plus the HC control parameter length. The packet type is also needed because the control parameter indications are not unique across HC schemes, which is why the PW type identifies the scheme.
sections.eli5: Every package gets a tiny tag saying what kind of package it is and, if it is small, how long it is, so padding cannot confuse the receiver.

sections.title: Packet Reordering
sections.content: Lossy or reordering paths need care. CRTP was designed for reliable point-to-point links with short delays and does not perform well with high packet loss, reordering and long delays, though it is still the choice in many cases. ECRTP can be considered for more robustness, since it repeats updates and sends absolute values in addition to deltas. The RFC advises that IPHC should use TCP_NODELTA, ECRTP should send absolute values, and ROHC should be adapted as discussed in RFC 4224.
sections.eli5: If letters might arrive out of order, it helps to write the full address on some of them instead of only the changes since the last letter.

sections.title: Worked Example: ECRTP Pseudowire
sections.content:
The RFC traces a bi-directional ECRTP pseudowire between R1/HC and R4/HD. Both are configured with the same 32-bit PW ID. R1/HC is set to receive up to 200 simultaneous ECRTP flows and R4/HD up to 255. R1/HC sends LDP Targeted Hello messages to UDP port 646, an LDP session is built over a TCP connection on port 646, and Label Mapping messages carry PW type 0x001B, the PW ID and the configuration sub-TLV. Once a router has sent and received Label Mapping messages with the same PW type and PW ID, it considers the PW established.

The data flow is G.729 voice with 20 bytes of payload per RTP packet. The first 3 packets go as FULL_HEADER with length 62 (2 + 20 + 8 + 12 + 20 bytes). The next 3 go as COMPRESSED_UDP_8 with length 36, and later packets as COMPRESSED_RTP_8 with length 26, all with the same MPLS label stack and CID.
sections.eli5: The example shows two routers shaking hands, then sending the first few messages in full, then shorter and shorter versions of the same message as both sides learn what stays the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The general MPLS pseudowire security considerations of RFC 3985 and RFC 4447 apply. This document specifies an encapsulation, not the protocols that carry the packets across the network or the protocols being encapsulated. Those protocols may have their own security issues, which the encapsulation does not affect. The security considerations of the supported HC protocols (RFC 2507, RFC 2508, RFC 3095 and RFC 3545) apply as well.
sections.eli5: This note only describes the envelope, so the safety rules of the envelope's contents and delivery routes still apply.
